lesson.title: Capital Allocation Line and Capital Market Line
lesson.summary: The capital allocation line shows every risk and return combination you can build by mixing a risk-free asset with one risky portfolio. The capital market line is the special case where that risky portfolio is the market portfolio, and its slope is the reward per unit of total risk.

sections.heading: Mixing safe and risky: the idea behind the CAL
sections.body_markdown:
Picture a dial that sets how much of your money goes into a savings account (the **risk-free asset**, with a return $R_f$ and zero standard deviation) and how much goes into one particular risky portfolio. Turn the dial and your portfolio's expected return and risk change together in a **straight line**. That line, drawn with standard deviation on the horizontal axis and expected return on the vertical axis, is the **capital allocation line (CAL)**.

The line starts at the risk-free rate on the vertical axis (zero risk) and runs through the risky portfolio. Putting more than 100% of your wealth into the risky portfolio, by borrowing at $R_f$, extends the line past that point.

Each risky portfolio has its own CAL. A different risky portfolio gives a different line.

$$E(R_p)=R_f+\frac{E(R_i)-R_f}{\sigma_i}\,\sigma_p$$

Here the risky portfolio is $i$, and $p$ is the mix of $i$ and the risk-free asset.

The mix is easy to compute. With weight $w$ in the risky portfolio and $1-w$ in the risk-free asset, $E(R_p)=wE(R_i)+(1-w)R_f$ and $\sigma_p=w\sigma_i$. The risk-free asset has zero standard deviation and zero correlation with everything, so risk scales in proportion to $w$.

The CAL does not depend on how much risk you want to take. Your risk appetite only decides where you sit on the line.

A useful comparison is a thermostat. Every setting uses the same heater, but you choose how high to turn it.

The weights $w$ and $1-w$ are fractions of your own wealth. Borrowing at the risk-free rate makes $w>1$ and $1-w<0$.

In this lesson, 'risk' on the horizontal axis means total risk, measured by standard deviation.

- $w<1$: you are **lending** (holding some risk-free asset).
- $w=1$: you hold the risky portfolio alone.
- $w>1$: you are **borrowing** at $R_f$ to leverage the risky portfolio.

The next section explains the slope.

Terms: *expected return* is the probability-weighted average return, and *standard deviation* is the usual measure of total risk.

The CAL is therefore a menu of choices, not a single portfolio.

An investor selects one point on it.

Which point is best depends on risk preferences, which are outside this LOS.

On the exam, remember that this line is drawn for a chosen risky portfolio and a risk-free rate.

The key is that the line is straight.

That straightness comes from the zero risk of the risk-free asset.

Without it, mixing two risky assets would give a curve, not a line.

The next section links the slope to the Sharpe ratio.

This is the exam-level idea.

Remember it.

Thanks to the zero-risk asset, return and risk grow in lockstep.

That is why the CAL is linear.

That is the whole logic.
